newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian politics seen on the boil as poll nears.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian politics seen on the boil as poll nears.

text.p: Deep-rooted suspicion and a bitter struggle for power within Cambodia's coalition government are almost certain to trigger political instability in the run-up to elections next year.

While pessimists fear that political rows could spark fighting, others are hopeful that pressure from Cambodia's regional partners will prevent the country from toppling over the brink into renewed warfare.
At the core of the crisis is a feud between the country's two prime ministers -- former battlefield foes -- who were thrown together in a coalition after the 1993 United Nations-run elections.
"The fundamental problem is a lack of power sharing," a Cambodian political analyst who declined to be identified said on Thursday.
"It has to do with the lack of trust and understanding," said another analyst, Kao Kim Hourn, director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace, a think tank.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, a son of King Norodom Sihanouk, led his royalist FUNCINPEC party from its jungle guerrilla bases to victory in the 1993 polls.
After a brief period of chaos, Ranariddh agreed to a coalition with Hun Sen, leader of the Vietnamese-backed communist government that ruled until a 1991 peace treaty officially ended the war.

For three years the coalition functioned as both premiers consolidated their strength. Economic liberalisation produced a degree of prosperity not seen for decades and the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group was decimated by defections and splits.

But relations between the two turned icy last year when Ranariddh demanded that Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party, which maintained a well-run and powerful political machine from its decade of government, give him greater powers.
Since the breakdown in their personal relations, virtually any difference between the men has the potential to explode into confrontation, analysts said.

"What you're seeing is a clash of values, a clash of interests between those who stayed through the rough times and those who came back and by some miracle, won (the election). The suspicion is still very much there and there's no relief in sight," said an Asian diplomat.
"Every challenge by Ranariddh is seen as provocation by Hun Sen," he said.
Political structures designed to foster reconciliation have proved unworkable with the two main parties at odds. Parliament has been deadlocked for weeks.

With little in the way of policy differences, both men are striving to bolster their strength in the run-up to the election with attempts to woo members of the rival camp and form alliances with small parties and with defecting Khmer Rouge units.
"The election is the big question mark," said a political source close to Hun Sen.
"Both see the 1998 election beckoning with the hope of absolute victory and the fear of total defeat with no limits to either," said another political analyst.

The two men have well-armed personal security forces and political sources say the danger is that a row might spark violence between the bodyguards, as has almost happened on several recent occasions, and that it could spread to units from the armed forces.

"I'm afraid this will continue, with ups and downs, until the election," said the Asian diplomat. "They seem to be always on the brink. The risk of an all-out civil war has been reduced but I would not rule out any sporadic clash."
Kao Kim Hourn said he hoped that Cambodia's gaining full membership in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in July will have a moderating influence on the feuding premiers.
Leaders of ASEAN, which now groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, have quietly been telling the premiers to sort out their differences.
"ASEAN has put a lot of pressure and will continue to do so. They will listen to the advice, but ultimately the question comes back to power politics and who's on top," another diplomat said.
